title: Demonstrating the baptizing walk, a tribute to Ellington and Bubbles
summary: Green says he wanted to be a stunt man, then performs his tap walk to Take the A Train as a courtesy to Ellington, from Bubbles' step to the diggings.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, I tried to eventually to become a stunt man and I was hoping someday to see where did they go to school. Where do -- where is the stuntman's school? That was always a, you know, a thinking I had. Where do they -- who are some of the stuntmen's teachers. I mean, what's their names? And, so, I guess it was the Maker that encouraged me -- "Once the task has begun, never leave it til it's done. Be the labor, great and small, never leave it, do it well -- and do it well or not at all." So, I taught this step, I mean, I've been taught by masters -- the father of rhythm, how to do the kick cramp, you know, the water fall wings. I say, "I think I want to try to baptize one of these steps -- these tap steps (unintelligible). At that time I was learning myself a walk -- a tap dancing walk, you see, and really that's exactly (unintelligible) that's what happened. I was baptizing a tap step, you know. Say, well, that dance, tap dancing must be some kind of joyful noise, so I'll keep it like that. This is what the people enjoyed. If you would like, I mean, I'll get up and arrive at this tap dancing walk and you'll hear how it goes. See, I tries to keep it in mind, and in the people's mind if they ever see it because of the melody, "A Train."
So, are you ready to do it, Chuck?
Yes, George.
Here we go.
This is dedicated to Duke, you would say this step?
Yes, this is my courtesy to him and his band.
(dancing)
That was dedicated to the one I love. (Recording interruption)
I know you'd have to have a lot of control to be able to do this walking tap as you call it.
Yes. That's exactly what it was. But you'd have to have a lot of control in order to baptize, that's what's the hard part.
Yes. I understand.
See, if you can baptize, you can always be respectful.
So, that's a Chuck Green original?
Yes. That's right.
You developed that -- everything is Chuck Green.
Yes.
You developed that whole style of that walking tap, as you call it?
Yes. That's what they call keeping it alive, you know, keeping it alive.
It You looked great and it sounds so great -- wonderful.
Yeah, it's from a step that John Bubbles used to do in Buck and Bubbles. He called it to the diggings.
So, this is the student complimenting his master?
Oh, yes, by all degrees.
Both masters, John Bubbles and Duke Ellington.
Yes.
And you loved them both.
Oh, yes, yeah.
It's a beautiful compliment.
Yes.
